title: Sleeping More Than Nine Hours Linked to Higher Alzheimer's Protein Levels
excerpt: Two new studies reveal that both sleep duration and genetic factors interact to shape Alzheimer's risk, with long sleep emerging as a potential early warning sign.
body:
• A UT Health San Antonio study of 2,410 participants found that regularly sleeping 8.5 to 9+ hours was associated with higher blood levels of p-tau181, an Alzheimer's biomarker
  • A separate Edith Cowan University study found that certain gene variants accelerate brain tissue loss in people who sleep less, suggesting a gene-sleep interaction in Alzheimer's risk
  • Researchers stress that the findings do not prove causation but suggest sleep patterns may serve as an early behavioural marker worth discussing with a doctor

Regularly sleeping nine or more hours a night is associated with higher levels of a key Alzheimer's disease protein in the blood, according to new research from UT Health San Antonio. The finding, published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, adds to growing evidence that sleep patterns—both too little and too much—may serve as early markers for neurodegeneration.

The Long Sleep Connection

Researchers analysed data from 2,410 participants in the Framingham Heart Study, an ongoing community-based cohort study. Using nonlinear statistical modelling, they found a J-shaped relationship between sleep duration and phosphorylated tau 181 (p-tau181), a modified protein that is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease and can now be detected through a blood test.

Participants who regularly slept 8.5 to 9 hours showed elevated p-tau181 levels, with the sharpest increase occurring beyond 10 hours of sleep. The association held even after researchers adjusted for age, sex, sleep apnea, depression, kidney function, and the APOE ε4 gene variant, a known genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's.

"When you force a straight line through data that curves, you miss the story entirely. We knew from the existing literature that the relationship between sleep and these biomarkers was unlikely to be simple, and that's exactly what we found."

— Dr. Vanessa M. Young, UT Health San Antonio

Three other brain-damage biomarkers tested did not show the same association once kidney function was accounted for, suggesting the link between long sleep and p-tau181 may be specific to Alzheimer's-related processes.

Genes and Sleep: A Two-Way Street

A separate study from Edith Cowan University in Australia, also published in Alzheimer's & Dementia, approached the sleep-Alzheimer's connection from a genetic angle. Researchers examined 13 common variants of the aquaporin-4 (AQP4) gene, which regulates fluid movement through the brain and supports its overnight waste-clearing system—the glymphatic pathway.

The study found that people carrying certain AQP4 variants showed faster grey matter loss when they reported shorter sleep. Others who took longer to fall asleep showed changes in brain structure linked to reduced brain volume. The direction and severity of these effects depended on which AQP4 variant a person carried.

"It's not just which genes you carry—it's how those genes interact with the world around you," said Dr. Ayeisha Milligan Armstrong. "The same variant can look protective or detrimental depending on how someone is sleeping."

What This Means in Practice

Both research teams emphasised that their findings do not establish that sleep directly causes Alzheimer's disease. Instead, abnormal sleep patterns may function as early behavioural signals—either reflecting underlying neurodegeneration already in progress or contributing to conditions that accelerate it.

Dementia affects 57 million people globally, with Alzheimer's accounting for 60% to 70% of cases. Identifying modifiable risk factors like sleep could enable earlier detection and potentially delay disease onset.

"If you regularly find yourself sleeping 9 to 10 hours or more a night, it may be worth mentioning to your doctor as a useful conversation starter about your sleep quality and overall brain health," said Dr. Young.

Previous research from UC San Diego also found that poor sleep quality was associated with worse memory and greater tau accumulation in older women with higher genetic risk for Alzheimer's. Women account for nearly two-thirds of Alzheimer's cases and frequently report poorer sleep quality than men, making sleep monitoring especially relevant for this group.

Practical Steps

While researchers caution against drawing direct conclusions, the emerging consensus points to sleep quality and duration as factors worth tracking. Adults experiencing persistent changes in sleep patterns—whether sleeping markedly longer or struggling with fragmented sleep—may benefit from discussing these patterns with their healthcare provider. Sleep tracking devices and apps can help document patterns over time for clinical review.

The research also reinforces the importance of addressing known sleep disruptors, including sleep apnea, depression, and irregular schedules, all of which can independently affect both sleep quality and brain health outcomes.
